content.title: Population, Sample, and Simple Random Sampling
content.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of populations and samples, specifically focusing on calculating the probability that a specific individual is included in a simple random sample (SRS).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between a population and a sample.
Define the characteristics of a simple random sample (SRS).
Calculate the inclusion probability for an individual in a sample drawn without replacement.
Calculate the inclusion probability for an individual in a sample drawn with replacement.

sections.title: Populations and Samples
sections.content: In statistics, the population (N) represents the entire group of individuals or items that we want to study. A sample (n) is a subset of that population actually selected for data collection. For a sample to be a 'Simple Random Sample' (SRS), every possible subset of size n must have an equal chance of being selected. This implies that every individual in the population has an equal probability of being included in the sample.

sections.title: Inclusion Probability: Without Replacement
sections.content: When sampling is conducted 'without replacement,' an individual cannot be selected more than once. Due to symmetry, the probability that any specific individual is included in the sample is simply the sample size (n) divided by the population size (N). The formula is: P(Inclusion) = n / N. Alternatively, this can be calculated using combinations by finding the probability of exclusion: P(Exclusion) = C(N-1, n) / C(N, n). The inclusion probability is then 1 - P(Exclusion).

sections.title: Inclusion Probability: With Replacement
sections.content:
When sampling is conducted 'with replacement,' an individual can be selected multiple times. In this scenario, the probability of being selected in a single draw is 1/N. The probability of NOT being selected in a single draw is (1 - 1/N). For a sample of size n, the probability of being excluded every single time is (1 - 1/N)^n. Therefore, the probability of being included at least once is: P(Inclusion) = 1 - (1 - 1/N)^n.

![A flowchart showing the steps to determine inclusion probability based on whether sampling is with or without replacement.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/c4b13b77-809f-4679-a411-5b23eedd88c5-1786506142840-368.webp)

worked_examples.question: A committee of 5 students is to be chosen at random from a class of 30 students without replacement. What is the probability that a specific student, Leo, is chosen for the committee?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the population size (N = 30) and the sample size (n = 5). Step 2: Confirm the sampling method is 'without replacement.' Step 3: Apply the symmetry rule for inclusion probability: P = n / N. Step 4: Calculate 5 / 30 = 1/6. The probability Leo is included is 1/6.

worked_examples.question: A bag contains 50 unique marbles. You draw 3 marbles one at a time, returning each marble to the bag before the next draw. What is the probability that the 'Gold' marble is selected at least once?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify N = 50 and n = 3. Step 2: Confirm the sampling method is 'with replacement.' Step 3: Calculate the probability of exclusion for one draw: 1 - (1/50) = 49/50. Step 4: Calculate the probability of exclusion for all 3 draws: (49/50)^3. Step 5: Subtract from 1 to find inclusion: 1 - (49/50)^3.

common_mistakes: Confusing the inclusion probability (n/N) with the exclusion probability (N-n)/N.
Applying the simple n/N formula to 'with replacement' scenarios where the math requires exponents.
Misidentifying the population size N by including the sample size n in the total count.
exam_tips: If the question asks for the probability of a specific individual being included in an SRS without replacement, look for the n/N fraction immediately.
Always check if the problem says 'with replacement' or 'without replacement' as this changes the formula.
Remember that in an SRS, every individual has the exact same probability of being chosen as every other individual.
content.recap: The population is the whole group (N), and the sample is the subset (n). In a simple random sample without replacement, the probability of any specific individual being included is n/N. If sampling with replacement, the probability is 1 - (1 - 1/N)^n.

knowledge_claims.content: The population (N) is the complete set of all individuals or items under study.
A sample (n) is a subset of the population selected for observation or analysis.
In a simple random sample (SRS), every possible subset of size n has an equal probability of being selected.
For a simple random sample without replacement, the probability that a specific individual is included is n / N.
Symmetry in an SRS without replacement ensures that every individual in the population has the same inclusion probability.
To calculate inclusion probability without replacement using the complement, subtract the probability of exclusion [C(N-1, n) / C(N, n)] from 1.
For sampling with replacement, the probability a specific individual is included at least once in n draws is 1 - (1 - 1/N)^n.
It is a mistake to use the formula n/N for sampling with replacement; this formula only applies to sampling without replacement.
When calculating inclusion probability, verify that N represents the total population and n represents the number of individuals selected.

Sampling without replacement results in a higher inclusion probability for a single individual than sampling with replacement for the same n and N, because the individual cannot be 'wasted' on multiple draws.
The term 'without replacement' indicates that once an item is selected, it is removed from the population and cannot be selected again in that sample.
If a population has 100 members and a sample of 5 is drawn without replacement, any specific member has a 5/100 (or 1/20) chance of being selected.

items.stem: A school surveys only students leaving the gym to estimate weekly exercise for all students. What is the primary concern?

options.F: The sample is random because participants were easy to find.
options.G: The sampling method may overrepresent people connected to the activity being measured.
options.H: A survey can never be used to estimate a population value.
options.J: The response variable must be measured in centimeters.

items.explanation: A convenience sample drawn from a relevant location can systematically differ from the target population.
